Title: From sinew to horn: The rise of composite bow in ancient warfare | Jordan Times
# From sinew to horn: The rise of composite bow in ancient warfare. AMMAN — Among the oldest and most effective weapons of antiquity were simple and composite bows. Scholars have studied the transition from simple to composite bows, highlighting key advancements. "The second type of simple bow, known as the double-convex or sinew-reinforced bow, gets its name from its distinct shape," explained Professor Aaron Burke. The next major advancement was the composite bow, achieved by adding a horn to the other side of the double-convex bow. "Thanks to the tensile strength of the composite bow, the arms bent backwards when unstrung, a characteristic known as a reflex," Burke noted. Burke pointed out that the best evidence for the use of composite bows in the ancient Near East comes from numerous arrowheads of varying weights and designs. The use of heavier arrows is supported by depictions of Amenhotep II and other New Kingdom pharaohs, shown firing arrows (likely bronze) through thick copper targets with composite bows. "The composite bow was also employed for rapid firing of lighter arrows, with modern experiments suggesting that an expert archer could shoot around thirty arrows in just three minutes," Burke noted. "In northern Mesopotamia, the composite bow likely replaced the simple bow as early as the Early Bronze Age.". One significant depiction of the composite bow is found in the pre-Sargonic palace at Mari (circa 2300 BCE), where the double-curved reflexed composite bow is shown. Yadin referred to this as the “Scythian bow” because it was previously associated with the Scythians of the late Iron Age. Further evidence for the composite bow includes depictions of fragments of Akkadian stelae. One such stele shows Naram-Sin depicted as a god, holding a composite bow and a battle axe in his left arm. Secondary archaeological evidence for the bow includes arrowheads and the casualties they caused during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages. "Although arrowheads from Anatolia and Mesopotamia from these periods are abundant, evidence for the use of either the simple or composite bow in the Levant during the Middle Bronze Age remains ambiguous," Burke said. ## {{articles\_filter\_1623\_widget.title}}. {{ articles\_filter\_1623[0]?.title }}. {{ articles\_filter\_1623[1]?.title }}. ### {{articles\_filter\_1746[0]?.title}}. ### {{articles\_filter\_1747[0]?.title}}. ### {{articles\_filter\_1748[0]?.title}}. .related-articles .article-widget-sm .article-title{font-size:16px;-webkit-line-clamp:3;} .related-articles .layout-ratio{padding-bottom:55%;}.

results.title: The Composite Bow: The Medieval Precursor to the Rifle
results.content: ***The composite bow, which created and destroyed empires, was the most effective of medieval weapons before the advent of the gun.***. These ancient soldiers had been hit by the deadly fire of the preeminent weapon of the day, the composite bow. Sleek and graceful, accurate and powerful, a masterful combination of natural products and human ingenuity, the composite bow emerged from the kingdoms of ancient Mesopotamia to revolutionize war-making for millennia and bring about the rise and fall of empires. Significantly, this new divinity’s weapon of choice was the composite bow. Only special types of carefully selected sinew, wood, and horn were suitable for making composite bows. An additional advantage was that the composite bow’s arrows were of lighter construction, which meant that an archer could carry many more of them and thus remain in the field longer. As far as is known, the first people to successfully wield composite bows in battle were the urban Akkadians, a people who ruled the world’s first empire from their capital city, Akkad, located in present-day Iraq. Moreover, weapon systems radically changed, for the composite bow was perfectly suited to be fired from the ultimate shock-weapon of the day, the chariot, which led to the chariot becoming a major wing of ancient armies, such as those of the Assyrians, Hittites, and Egyptians. When these kingdoms waned, the Neo-Assyrian Empire arose, making good use of the composite bow with its huge chariot forces. When Neo-Assyrian chariots were phased out in favor of cheaper, more flexible cavalry troops, the composite bow remained the principle weapon. Despite differences in language, customs, and histories, all of these peoples, kingdoms, and empires shared one thing in common: the use of the composite bow as their definitive weapon. Interestingly, the composite bow never found favor among the empires of the West. Brandished by divine heroes, wielded by bronze-clad warriors in chariots, the decisive weapon on battlefields from Japan to North America, present at the creation of empires and instrumental in their ruin, the composite bow was arguably the most effective weapon in existence before the advent of the gun. A composite bow is expensive to make and requires training.

results.title: The history of the composite bow - Bow International
results.content: # The history of the composite bow. Rather than being straight, like wooden self bows, composite bows are usually recurved, their reflex tips pointing away from the archer in an unstrung state. *Composite bows come in all shapes and sizes. Since horn, wood and sinew are all natural and, hence, perishable materials, only very little archaeological evidence remains of the existence of early composite bows. Despite its use of space-age materials, such as aluminium, glass fibre and carbon, fast-drying synthetic glues and features such as pistol grips and arrow shelves, the modern laminated recurve bow is essentially still a late descendant of the composite bow and makes use of the same mechanical principles. Nowadays, however, more and more bowyers all over the world are rediscovering the old methods and are once more building true composite bows in the Scythian, Turkish, Mongolian or Korean styles, using nothing but horn, sinew, wood, leather, bark and animal glue to keep the tradition alive. Title: Mastering Ancient Bow Making: The Art of Powerful Craft
# Ancient Bow Making: Crafting the Legendary Composite Bow. Ancient bow making was a revered craft, blending artistry and engineering to create weapons that shaped history. Jonathan’s fascination with bows began as he observed Roman archers and skilled bowyers in Crete, where composite bows were crafted with remarkable expertise. ## The Composite Bow: A Masterpiece of Materials. Composite bows were ingeniously constructed from a combination of wood, horn, and sinew—each material chosen for its unique mechanical properties. The composite bow’s layered design allowed it to store and release more energy than a simple wooden bow, resulting in greater power and range. This compactness did not sacrifice power, making composite bows ideal for the varied demands of Roman military campaigns. Crafting a composite bow was no simple task. ## The Role of Composite Bows in Roman Military and Hunting. Roman archers relied heavily on composite bows for their effectiveness in warfare. Composite bows allowed Roman archers to engage enemies at a distance while also providing sustenance through hunting, demonstrating the bow’s versatility and importance in ancient military logistics. ## The Coveted Antelope Horn: Why It Was Essential in Ancient Bow Making. In the final chapters of the book, Jonathan is gifted an antelope horn—a highly prized material in the craft of ancient bow making. This gift reflects not only respect but also the critical role animal horns played in creating powerful composite bows. This unique composition gives the horn exceptional compressive strength and elasticity, allowing it to withstand the intense bending and compressive forces experienced on the belly (the side facing the archer) of a composite bow. The composite bow remains a symbol of human ingenuity, where natural materials and skilled hands combine to create tools that have shaped history. For those who have completed the story, we invite you to join The Potter’s Story Reader’s Circle, where exclusive content delves into the deeper symbolism of creating composite bows that Jonathan was bent on mastering. This members-only content offers detailed insights into how ancient bow making reflects the character’s journey and commentary on how the craft serves as both a literal skill and a profound metaphor throughout the story.
